claim: De novo-designed transmembrane domains (TMDs) can be used to tune engineered receptor functions.
source: De novo-designed receptor transmembrane domains (TMDs) present opportunities for precise control of cellular receptor functions.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this as the main premise of the work.

claim: A de novo design strategy was developed for generating programmed membrane proteins (proMPs) that are single-pass α-helical TMDs.
source: We developed a de novo design strategy for generating programmed membrane proteins (proMPs): single-pass α-helical TMDs that self-assemble through computationally defined and crystallographically validated interfaces.
evidence: The abstract describes the development of the design strategy and characterization of the resulting proteins.

claim: proMPs self-assemble through computationally defined and crystallographically validated interfaces.
source: We developed a de novo design strategy for generating programmed membrane proteins (proMPs): single-pass α-helical TMDs that self-assemble through computationally defined and crystallographically validated interfaces.
evidence: The abstract states that the interfaces were both computationally designed and experimentally validated by crystallography.

claim: CAR T cell cytokine release in vitro scales linearly with the oligomeric state encoded by the receptor TMD from monomers up to tetramers.
source: We used these proMPs to program specific oligomeric interactions into a chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) that we expressed in mouse primary T cells and found that both in vitro CAR T cell cytokine release and in vivo antitumor activity scaled linearly with the oligomeric state encoded by the receptor TMD, from monomers up to tetramers.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding from experimental data.

claim: In vivo antitumor activity of CAR T cells scales linearly with the oligomeric state encoded by the receptor TMD from monomers up to tetramers.
source: We used these proMPs to program specific oligomeric interactions into a chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) that we expressed in mouse primary T cells and found that both in vitro CAR T cell cytokine release and in vivo antitumor activity scaled linearly with the oligomeric state encoded by the receptor TMD, from monomers up to tetramers.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding from in vivo experimental data.

claim: All programmed CARs stimulated substantially lower T cell cytokine release relative to the commonly used CD28 TMD.
source: All programmed CARs stimulated substantially lower T cell cytokine release relative to the commonly used CD28 TMD, which we show elevated cytokine release through lateral recruitment of the endogenous T cell costimulatory receptor CD28.
evidence: The abstract states this as a finding from experimental data comparing proCAR constructs to CD28 TMD-containing CARs.

claim: The CD28 TMD elevates cytokine release through lateral recruitment of the endogenous T cell costimulatory receptor CD28.
source: All programmed CARs stimulated substantially lower T cell cytokine release relative to the commonly used CD28 TMD, which we show elevated cytokine release through lateral recruitment of the endogenous T cell costimulatory receptor CD28.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this mechanism was demonstrated in the study.

claim: Transmembrane domains govern key interactions involved in assembly, activation, and high-order clustering in immune receptors, death receptors, and growth factor receptors.
source: In immune receptors (Berry and Call, 2017; Dong et al., 2019), death receptors (Fu et al., 2016; Pan et al., 2019), and growth factor receptors (Arkhipov et al., 2013; Endres et al., 2013; Fleishman et al., 2002), the transmembrane domains (TMDs) govern key interactions involved in assembly, activation, and high-order clustering.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Control over the specificity, stability, geometry, and oligomeric state of TMD interactions is highly desirable for mechanistic studies of natural receptors and engineering of synthetic receptors.
source: Control over the specificity, stability, geometry, and oligomeric state of these interactions is therefore highly desirable both for mechanistic studies of natural receptors and in the engineering of synthetic receptors.
evidence: This is stated as a motivation for the work based on the importance of TMD properties.

claim: Accurate control of TMD properties is difficult to achieve using natural TMDs that have likely been evolutionarily selected for flexibility.
source: Accurate control, however, is difficult to achieve using natural TMDs that have likely been evolutionarily selected for a degree of flexibility in these very attributes (Matthews et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and represents a challenge addressed by the work.

claim: CAR T cell therapies have been clinically adopted for cancer immunotherapy.
source: The importance of high precision in receptor engineering has come into particularly sharp focus with the clinical adoption of cancer immunotherapies using targeted chimeric antigen receptors (CARs) (Majzner and Mackall, 2019; June et al., 2018; Salter et al., 2018; Eshhar et al., 1993) to endow T cells with potent antitumor activity.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Controlling functional outputs from engineered single-chain immune receptors poses significant challenges in balancing antitumor CAR T cell activity against toxicities associated with cytokine release syndrome.
source: Controlling functional outputs from these engineered single-chain immune receptors poses significant challenges in balancing antitumor CAR T cell activity against toxicities associated with high inflammatory cytokine release, known as cytokine release syndrome (CRS) (Morgan et al., 2010; Gutierrez et al., 2018; Morris et al., 2022; Maus et al., 2020).
evidence: This challenge is stated with supporting citations to the literature on CRS.

claim: Current-generation CARs comprise an antibody single-chain variable fragment (scFv) domain for tumor antigen binding, a spacer or hinge domain for length and flexibility, a TMD controlling membrane integration and expression levels, and intracellular costimulation and activation domains.
source: Current-generation CARs comprise an antibody single-chain variable fragment (scFv) domain for tumor antigen binding, a spacer or hinge domain for length and flexibility, a TMD controlling membrane integration and expression levels, and intracellular costimulation and activation domains that provide signals for proliferation, survival, and activation of T cell effector functions.
evidence: This describes the established modular structure of CAR constructs.

claim: Most CAR TMDs incorporate the TMD sequence of the protein from which the adjacent hinge or signaling domains were derived, most commonly from CD4, CD8, CD28, or CD3ζ.
source: For convenience, most incorporate the TMD sequence of the protein from which the adjacent hinge or signaling domains were derived; that is, most commonly from endogenous T cell proteins such as CD4, CD8, CD28, or the T cell receptor (TCR)-associated CD3ζ chain.
evidence: This describes common practice in CAR design.

claim: Some natural TMD sequences used in CARs can engage in molecular interactions that drive self-association and/or assembly with endogenous T cell proteins, impacting CAR expression and functions.
source: At least some of these TMD sequences can engage in molecular interactions that drive self-association and/or assembly with the essential T cell proteins from which they were derived and thereby impact CAR expression and functions in ways that reduce control over signaling outcomes (Bridgeman et al., 2010; Cosson et al., 1991; Leddon et al., 2020; Call et al., 2006; Hennecke and Cosson, 1993; Muller et al., 2021; Bridgeman et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Natural immune receptor TMDs in CARs may contribute to enhanced function by driving CAR homodimer formation.
source: These may contribute to enhanced function by, for example, driving CAR homodimer formation (Salzer et al., 2020; Bridgeman et al., 2010; Fujiwara et al., 2020), but the involvement of natural immune receptor TMDs in native T cell signaling hampers rational design of CARs with predictable properties.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The involvement of natural immune receptor TMDs in native T cell signaling hampers rational design of CARs with predictable properties.
source: These may contribute to enhanced function by, for example, driving CAR homodimer formation (Salzer et al., 2020; Bridgeman et al., 2010; Fujiwara et al., 2020), but the involvement of natural immune receptor TMDs in native T cell signaling hampers rational design of CARs with predictable properties.
evidence: This is stated as a problem motivating the use of de novo designed TMDs.

claim: Limitations of membrane protein atomistic calculations have restricted de novo α-helical MP design studies to highly predictable and rigid coiled-coil motifs.
source: Despite significant recent progress (Barth and Senes, 2016; Korendovych and DeGrado, 2020), the limitations of membrane protein (MP) atomistic calculations have restricted de novo ɑ-helical MP design studies to highly predictable and rigid coiled-coil motifs (Joh et al., 2014; Lu et al., 2018) that, while stabilizing them, limited their usefulness as receptor TMDs.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work in the field.

claim: An ab initio Rosetta atomistic modeling strategy uses a new energy function with experimentally determined membrane-solvation terms for each amino acid.
source: By contrast, we recently described an ab initio Rosetta atomistic modeling strategy (Weinstein et al., 2019) that uses a new energy function with experimentally determined membrane-solvation terms for each amino acid.
evidence: This describes a previously published method by the authors.

claim: The Rosetta modeling strategy accurately predicts the structure of single-spanning sequences known to self-assemble.
source: This modeling strategy accurately predicts the structure of single-spanning sequences known to self-assemble (Elazar et al., 2016a; Elazar et al., 2016b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior validation work.

claim: proCARs maintained significantly lower inflammatory cytokine release compared to an otherwise identical CAR containing the natural CD28 TMD.
source: proCARs also maintained significantly lower inflammatory cytokine release compared to an otherwise identical CAR containing the natural CD28 TMD, a property that may have safety benefits in clinical applications (Brudno et al., 2020; Ying et al., 2019; Morris et al., 2022; Rafiq et al., 2020; Alabanza et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study with citations supporting the potential clinical relevance.

claim: Lower inflammatory cytokine release may have safety benefits in clinical CAR T cell applications.
source: proCARs also maintained significantly lower inflammatory cytokine release compared to an otherwise identical CAR containing the natural CD28 TMD, a property that may have safety benefits in clinical applications (Brudno et al., 2020; Ying et al., 2019; Morris et al., 2022; Rafiq et al., 2020; Alabanza et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as a potential implication supported by citations.

claim: Round 1 design sequences were biased towards the hydrophobic amino acid leucine relative to naturally occurring TMDs.
source: We noticed that the resulting sequences were overwhelmingly biased towards the large and flexible hydrophobic amino acid Leu (Figure 1b), as expected from the dominant role of lipophilicity in the ref2015_memb potential (Weinstein et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1b comparing amino acid composition.

claim: Forward-folding ab initio structure-prediction calculations indicated that round 1 designs were prone to form multiple alternative low-energy dimer structures different from the design conception.
source: Forward-folding ab initio structure-prediction calculations, however, indicated that the designs were prone to form multiple alternative low-energy dimer structures that were conformationally different from the design conception (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1a.

claim: A sequence diversification step comprising 120 iterations of single-point mutation and energy relaxation was introduced to mitigate the risk of misfolding.
source: To mitigate the risk of misfolding due to the high Leu content, we introduced a sequence diversification step comprising 120 iterations of single-point mutation and energy relaxation while biasing the sequence composition to match that of natural TMDs (Figure 1b; Equations 2-3).
evidence: This describes a methodological step taken in the design process.

claim: After sequence diversification, the resulting sequences converged to the design models in ab initio structure prediction calculations.
source: The resulting sequences were subjected to ab initio structure prediction calculations (Das et al., 2009), and this time, they converged to the design models (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b) and exhibited a large energy gap from undesired structures.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Natural TMDs are not optimized for thermodynamic stability.
source: Previous studies noted that natural TMDs are not optimized for thermodynamic stability (Faham et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated as prior knowledge with a citation.

claim: Evolution might have selected sequence compositions in natural TMDs to counter TMD misfolding.
source: Our design simulations suggest that evolution might have selected sequence compositions to counter TMD misfolding.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the computational results.

claim: Most proMPs supported high survival in the E. coli TOXCAT-β-lactamase selection system.
source: Remarkably, most proMPs supported high survival (Figure 1c) and two-thirds survived even at the highest chloramphenicol concentration tested, indicating a self-association strength significantly greater than the TMD from the human receptor-tyrosine kinase HER2 (also known as ErbB2), which served as a positive control.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1c.

claim: Two-thirds of proMPs survived even at the highest chloramphenicol concentration tested, indicating self-association strength significantly greater than the HER2 TMD.
source: Remarkably, most proMPs supported high survival (Figure 1c) and two-thirds survived even at the highest chloramphenicol concentration tested, indicating a self-association strength significantly greater than the TMD from the human receptor-tyrosine kinase HER2 (also known as ErbB2), which served as a positive control.
evidence: This is stated in the text with reference to Figure 1c showing the experimental data.

claim: Deep mutational scanning showed that the sensitivity to mutations of most designs was consistent with interfacial versus exposed positions in the design models.
source: Deep mutational scanning of mutant libraries showed that the sensitivity to mutations of most designs was consistent with interfacial versus exposed positions in the design models (Figure 1d–f, Figure 1—figure supplement 3), suggesting that they indeed assembled through the designed interfaces in the bacterial inner membrane.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figures 1d-f and Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Eight proMPs were produced recombinantly as free peptides and all exhibited electrophoretic mobility consistent with SDS- and heat-stable self-association.
source: Eight proMPs were produced recombinantly as free peptides and all exhibited electrophoretic mobility consistent with SDS- and heat-stable self-association (Figure 1g, Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1g and Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Six proMPs had the apparent molecular weight of a dimer and exhibited reduced mobility as the peptide concentration was increased.
source: Six proMPs had the apparent molecular weight of a dimer (e.g., proMP 1.5 and 1.6, Figure 1g) and exhibited reduced mobility as the peptide concentration was increased, similar to the SDS-stable (Lemmon et al., 1992) behavior of the well-studied glycophorin A TMD (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1g and Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Two proMPs exhibited migration patterns independent of sample concentration with apparent molecular weights more consistent with oligomers larger than dimers.
source: By contrast, the remaining two proMPs exhibited migration patterns that were independent of the sample concentration and had apparent molecular weights more consistent with oligomers larger than the designed dimers (proMP 1.2, Figure 1g; proMP 1.3, Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1g and Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The structure of proMP 1.2 was determined to 2.55 Å resolution.
source: To establish the molecular structures of these designs, several were screened for crystallization in monoolein lipid cubic phase, and the structure of proMP 1.2 was determined to 2.55 Å resolution (Figure 1h, Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1h and Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: proMP 1.2 formed a trimer instead of the intended dimer.
source: While the positions involved in helix packing recapitulated the design model, this proMP indeed formed a trimer instead of the intended dimer, indicating good concordance between mobility in SDS-PAGE and the oligomeric state solved by X-ray crystallography.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the crystal structure.

claim: There is good concordance between mobility in SDS-PAGE and the oligomeric state solved by X-ray crystallography for proMP 1.2.
source: While the positions involved in helix packing recapitulated the design model, this proMP indeed formed a trimer instead of the intended dimer, indicating good concordance between mobility in SDS-PAGE and the oligomeric state solved by X-ray crystallography.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from comparing SDS-PAGE and crystallographic data.

claim: Ab initio structure prediction calculations in trimeric (C3) symmetry recapitulated the experimentally observed packing interface of proMP 1.2 with RMSD 2.3 Å.
source: Ab initio structure prediction calculations in trimeric (C3) symmetry recapitulated the experimentally observed packing interface (RMSD 2.3 Å) (Figure 1h and i), demonstrating that it would have been possible to predict this outcome had we considered alternative oligomeric states during design calculations.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1h and i.

claim: It would have been possible to predict the trimeric outcome of proMP 1.2 had alternative oligomeric states been considered during design calculations.
source: Ab initio structure prediction calculations in trimeric (C3) symmetry recapitulated the experimentally observed packing interface (RMSD 2.3 Å) (Figure 1h and i), demonstrating that it would have been possible to predict this outcome had we considered alternative oligomeric states during design calculations.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the computational validation.

claim: A third design campaign incorporated a final step in which ab initio structure prediction calculations were performed in C2, C3, and C4 symmetries for every design.
source: Based on this insight, we initiated a third design campaign to produce proMPs in a range of oligomeric states. We incorporated a final step in which ab initio structure prediction calculations (Weinstein et al., 2019) were performed in C2, C3, and C4 symmetries for every design.
evidence: This describes a methodological improvement in the design process.

claim: Only proMPs predicted to form the target oligomeric state and none of the alternatives were selected for further analysis in the third design campaign.
source: Only those proMPs that were predicted to form the target oligomeric state and none of the alternatives were selected for further analysis (Figure 2a–d).
evidence: This describes the selection criteria used in the design process.

claim: Crystal structures were obtained confirming the target oligomeric state for two proMPs: a dimer (proMP C2.1) and a trimer (proMP C3.1).
source: This strategy yielded two proMPs for which we obtained crystal structures confirming the target oligomeric state: a dimer with glycine-based packing interface similar to the motif observed in human glycophorin A (proMP C2.1; Figure 2a–b and e–g, Figure 2—figure supplement 1), and a trimer with an alanine-rich interface that, to the best of our knowledge, is novel in a membrane protein (proMP C3.1; Figure 2c–d and h–k, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figures 2a-k and supplements.

claim: proMP C2.1 has a glycine-based packing interface similar to the motif observed in human glycophorin A.
source: This strategy yielded two proMPs for which we obtained crystal structures confirming the target oligomeric state: a dimer with glycine-based packing interface similar to the motif observed in human glycophorin A (proMP C2.1; Figure 2a–b and e–g, Figure 2—figure supplement 1), and a trimer with an alanine-rich interface that, to the best of our knowledge, is novel in a membrane protein (proMP C3.1; Figure 2c–d and h–k, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in the figures.

claim: proMP C3.1 has an alanine-rich interface that is novel in a membrane protein.
source: This strategy yielded two proMPs for which we obtained crystal structures confirming the target oligomeric state: a dimer with glycine-based packing interface similar to the motif observed in human glycophorin A (proMP C2.1; Figure 2a–b and e–g, Figure 2—figure supplement 1), and a trimer with an alanine-rich interface that, to the best of our knowledge, is novel in a membrane protein (proMP C3.1; Figure 2c–d and h–k, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in the figures.

claim: In the crystal structure of proMP C3.1, two of the helices aligned well with the design model while the third was in an antiparallel orientation.
source: Interestingly, while two of the helices in the crystal structure of proMP C3.1 aligned well with the design model (Figure 2i), the third was in an antiparallel orientation (Figure 2j).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2i and j.

claim: Despite the antiparallel arrangement in the crystal, the six key interface alanine β-methyls in proMP C3.1 were in near-identical positions to their counterparts in the fully parallel model.
source: Despite this arrangement, the six key interface alanine β-methyls were in near-identical positions to their counterparts in the fully parallel model (Figure 2k), leading us to suspect that the model is correct but the crystal lattice was enforcing the antiparallel binding mode of the third helix.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2k.

claim: The design model of proMP C3.1 cannot be accommodated in the crystal lattice due to clashes.
source: To probe this possibility, we aligned the parallel model with the asymmetric unit seen in the crystal structure and generated crystallographic symmetry. The resulting model showed clashes for the third helix and indicated that the design model cannot be accommodated in the crystal lattice.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from computational analysis of the crystal packing.

claim: proMP C3.1 is unintentionally 'reversible' in that one of the helices can form the intended packing mode in either orientation.
source: The structure thus suggests that this proMP is unintentionally 'reversible' in that one of the helices can form the intended packing mode in either orientation.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the structural data.

claim: Only the fully parallel trimer of proMP C3.1 can form in a biological system where the topology of a single-spanning TMD is constrained by biosynthetic machinery in a type I orientation.
source: While this feature is of interest from a design standpoint (Woodall et al., 2015), we note that only the fully parallel trimer depicted in the model can form in a biological system where the topology of a single-spanning TMD is constrained by the biosynthetic machinery in a type I orientation.
evidence: This is stated as an inference based on biological constraints.

claim: The sequence diversification and computational selection of oligomeric state provide a practical approach to implement negative design principles critical for accurate de novo TMD design.
source: We conclude that the sequence diversification and the computational selection of the oligomeric state described above provide a practical approach to implement negative design principles that are critical for accurate de novo TMD design (Fleishman and Baker, 2012; Joh et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the design work with supporting citations.

claim: These new insights will likely be critical to design de novo hetero-oligomeric TMDs.
source: These new insights will likely also be critical to design de novo hetero-oligomeric TMDs.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation about future applications.

claim: Both CD8 and CD28 TMDs drive disulfide-linked receptor homodimer formation in FDA-approved CAR T cell products.
source: The hinge-TMD regions in all CARs used in FDA-approved CAR T cell products derive from CD8 or CD28 and drive disulfide-linked receptor homodimer formation (Fujiwara et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: The importance of the dimeric state for optimal CAR function is not well understood.
source: However, the importance of the dimeric state for optimal CAR function is not well understood and alternative oligomeric forms such as trimers or tetramers have not been explored.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap motivating the study.

claim: Alternative oligomeric forms such as trimers or tetramers have not been explored for CARs.
source: However, the importance of the dimeric state for optimal CAR function is not well understood and alternative oligomeric forms such as trimers or tetramers have not been explored.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap.

claim: Both CD8 and CD28 TMDs have documented propensities to self-associate.
source: Furthermore, both CD8 and CD28 TMDs have documented propensities to self-associate (Hennecke and Cosson, 1993; Leddon et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: Use of CD8 or CD28 TMDs in CARs risks unintended interactions with native receptors that could affect CAR expression and/or function.
source: Given the presence of both native receptors in CAR T cells, their use in CARs risks unintended interactions that could affect their expression and/or function.
evidence: This is stated as a concern motivating the use of orthogonal proMPs.

claim: proCAR-2 and proCAR-3 were designed to form dimers and trimers, respectively.
source: To program CARs that form specific oligomeric states and are insulated from confounding interactions with endogenous signaling proteins, we initially chose the crystallographically confirmed proMPs C2.1 and 1.2 to generate proCARs that form dimers or trimers. These were termed proCAR-2 and proCAR-3, respectively (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3a.

claim: A monomeric proMP exhibited no chloramphenicol survival in dsTβL assays.
source: We also designed a monomeric proMP that exhibited no chloramphenicol survival in deep sequencing TβL (dsTβL) assays (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) and used it to produce a monomeric proCAR-1 in order to extend the structure–function study.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The proCAR designs incorporated an anti-HER2 scFv (FRP5), human CD8α hinge sequence, a proMP-derived TMD, human CD28 costimulatory sequence, and human CD3ζ activating tail.
source: Our proCAR designs incorporated an anti-HER2 scFv (FRP5; Wels et al., 1992) fused to the human CD8α hinge sequence, a proMP-derived TMD, the human CD28 costimulatory sequence, and the human CD3ζ activating tail.
evidence: This describes the design of the proCAR constructs.

claim: The reference CAR contained the human CD28 TMD, approximating a domain configuration that has been extensively studied in vitro and in vivo.
source: Our reference CAR contained the human CD28 TMD for comparison, approximating a domain configuration that has been extensively studied in vitro and in vivo (Davenport et al., 2018; Davenport et al., 2015; Haynes et al., 2002).
evidence: This describes the reference construct with supporting citations.

claim: A cysteine residue in the CD8α hinge that mediates disulfide-bonded dimer formation was mutated to alanine in all proCAR constructs.
source: In all proCAR constructs, a cysteine residue in the CD8α hinge that mediates disulfide-bonded dimer formation was mutated to alanine (Figure 3a) to ensure that the designed TMDs were the primary determinants of oligomeric state.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3a.

claim: All proCAR constructs exhibited similar cell-surface levels when expressed in murine BW5147 thymoma cells.
source: The HER2 proCARs and reference CD28TM constructs were retrovirally expressed in murine BW5147 thymoma cells. All constructs exhibited similar cell-surface levels (Figure 3b), and the reference CD28TM CAR formed disulfide-linked dimers while the cysteine mutant reference (No Cys) and proCARs did not (Figure 3c).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3b.

claim: The reference CD28TM CAR formed disulfide-linked dimers while the cysteine mutant reference (No Cys) and proCARs did not.
source: The HER2 proCARs and reference CD28TM constructs were retrovirally expressed in murine BW5147 thymoma cells. All constructs exhibited similar cell-surface levels (Figure 3b), and the reference CD28TM CAR formed disulfide-linked dimers while the cysteine mutant reference (No Cys) and proCARs did not (Figure 3c).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3c.

claim: All CARs were competent to signal when co-cultured with HER2+ SKBR3 human breast adenocarcinoma cells.
source: All CARs were competent to signal when co-cultured with HER2+ SKBR3 human breast adenocarcinoma cells (Figure 3d and e).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3d and e.

claim: All CARs mediated antigen-dependent killing of MC57 mouse fibrosarcoma cells stably expressing HER2 in vitro when expressed in freshly isolated mouse CD8+ T cells.
source: When expressed in freshly isolated mouse CD8+ T cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 2a and b), all CARs mediated antigen-dependent killing of MC57 mouse fibrosarcoma cells stably expressing HER2 in vitro (Figure 3f).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3f.

claim: Only small differences in killing potency were apparent among the CARs, with proCAR-1 trending slightly less effective and proCAR-2 and -3 trending slightly more effective than reference CARs.
source: Only small differences in killing potency were apparent, with proCAR-1 trending slightly less effective than the reference CARs and proCAR-2 and -3 trending slightly more effective.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the killing assay data.

claim: In vitro cytokine production (IFNγ, IL-2, TNFα, and GM-CSF) was significantly lower in all proCARs, reduced by 2- to 10-fold on average compared to CD28TM CAR.
source: In vitro cytokine production (IFNγ, IL-2, TNFα, and GM-CSF), on the other hand, was significantly lower in all proCARs, reduced by 2- to 10-fold on average (Figure 3g).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3g.

claim: The reduced cytokine release in proCARs was not due to loss of the CD8α hinge-region disulfide bond.
source: This effect was not apparent in the CD28TM (No Cys) background and was therefore not due to loss of the CD8α hinge-region disulfide bond.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from comparing constructs with and without the disulfide bond.

claim: The CD28 TMD contains a highly conserved polar YxxxxT motif similar to the one that drives CD3ζ dimerization.
source: The CD28 TMD contains a highly conserved polar YxxxxT motif that is similar to the one that drives CD3ζ dimerization (Call et al., 2006) and is required for optimal dimerization and surface expression of native CD28 (Leddon et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: The CD28 YxxxxT sequence is required for optimal dimerization and surface expression of native CD28.
source: The CD28 TMD contains a highly conserved polar YxxxxT motif that is similar to the one that drives CD3ζ dimerization (Call et al., 2006) and is required for optimal dimerization and surface expression of native CD28 (Leddon et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: The CD28 YxxxxT sequence causes CARs containing the CD28 TMD to physically associate with the CD28 protein in T cells.
source: A recent study showed that the CD28 YxxxxT sequence also causes CARs containing the CD28 TMD to physically associate with the CD28 protein in T cells (Muller et al., 2021), but the functional consequences of this association for CAR signaling have not been explored.
evidence: This is stated with a citation to a recent study.

claim: The functional consequences of CD28 TMD association with endogenous CD28 for CAR signaling have not been explored prior to this study.
source: A recent study showed that the CD28 YxxxxT sequence also causes CARs containing the CD28 TMD to physically associate with the CD28 protein in T cells (Muller et al., 2021), but the functional consequences of this association for CAR signaling have not been explored.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap addressed by the study.

claim: Tyrosine, serine, and threonine in the YSLLVT sequence of CD28 TMD could all contribute to an interhelical hydrogen-bonding network.
source: We modeled this putative CD28TM interface on the ζζ structure (Call et al., 2006) and noted that tyrosine, serine, and threonine in the YSLLVT sequence could all contribute to an interhelical hydrogen-bonding network (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is stated based on computational modeling shown in Figure 4a.

claim: A CAR with CD28 TMD YSLLVT mutated to FALLVV was well expressed as a disulfide-linked homodimer at the cell surface.
source: We therefore generated a CAR in which this sequence was mutated to FALLVV, selectively eliminating the key hydrogen-bonding hydroxyl groups, for comparison to our proCAR and reference constructs. This CAR was well expressed as a disulfide-linked homodimer at the cell surface (Figure 4b and c) and generated primary mouse CD8+ CAR T cells whose ability to kill HER2+ target cells in vitro was unimpaired (Figure 4d).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4b and c.

claim: The CD28TM mutant (FALLVV) generated primary mouse CD8+ CAR T cells whose ability to kill HER2+ target cells in vitro was unimpaired.
source: We therefore generated a CAR in which this sequence was mutated to FALLVV, selectively eliminating the key hydrogen-bonding hydroxyl groups, for comparison to our proCAR and reference constructs. This CAR was well expressed as a disulfide-linked homodimer at the cell surface (Figure 4b and c) and generated primary mouse CD8+ CAR T cells whose ability to kill HER2+ target cells in vitro was unimpaired (Figure 4d).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4d.

claim: The CD28TM mutant induced lower levels of cytokine secretion (two- to sixfold lower on average) similar to those observed for the proCARs.
source: The CD28TM mutant, however, induced lower levels of cytokine secretion (two- to sixfold lower on average; Figure 4d) that were similar to those observed for the proCARs.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4d.

claim: The low-cytokine release seen in the proCAR T cells was likely due to the proCARs being insulated from interaction with endogenous T cell signaling proteins, primarily CD28.
source: We therefore concluded that the low-cytokine release seen in the proCAR T cells was likely due to the proCARs being insulated from interaction with endogenous T cell signaling proteins, primarily CD28.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the mutant CAR experiments.

claim: Receptors containing the WT CD28 TMD frequently co-clustered endogenous surface CD28 in primary CD8+ T cells.
source: To directly interrogate potential CAR-CD28 associations in primary CD8+ T cells, we examined the four CAR constructs we expect to form dimers in a co-clustering experiment by fluorescence microscopy; these dimers included the CD28TM reference and CD28TM mutant as well as those that ablate the disulfide linkage for comparison (No Cys and proCAR-2). We found that receptors containing the WT CD28 TMD frequently co-clustered endogenous surface CD28, while the CD28TM mutant and proCAR-2 did so significantly less frequently (Figure 4e and f).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4e and f.

claim: The CD28TM mutant and proCAR-2 co-clustered with endogenous CD28 significantly less frequently than WT CD28 TMD CARs.
source: To directly interrogate potential CAR-CD28 associations in primary CD8+ T cells, we examined the four CAR constructs we expect to form dimers in a co-clustering experiment by fluorescence microscopy; these dimers included the CD28TM reference and CD28TM mutant as well as those that ablate the disulfide linkage for comparison (No Cys and proCAR-2). We found that receptors containing the WT CD28 TMD frequently co-clustered endogenous surface CD28, while the CD28TM mutant and proCAR-2 did so significantly less frequently (Figure 4e and f).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4e and f.

claim: The CD28TM interaction motif YSxxxT is linked to high cytokine production in CARs that incorporate this sequence.
source: These experiments clearly link the CD28TM interaction motif YSxxxT to high cytokine production in CARs that incorporate this sequence and implicate the recruitment of additional co-stimulatory signaling via endogenous T cell CD28 as the cause.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the co-clustering and functional experiments.

claim: Recruitment of additional co-stimulatory signaling via endogenous T cell CD28 is the cause of high cytokine production in CD28 TMD-containing CARs.
source: These experiments clearly link the CD28TM interaction motif YSxxxT to high cytokine production in CARs that incorporate this sequence and implicate the recruitment of additional co-stimulatory signaling via endogenous T cell CD28 as the cause.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the experiments.

claim: The de novo-designed TMDs are insulated from specific interactions with endogenous CD28.
source: They further substantiate that the de novo-designed TMDs are insulated from these specific interactions.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the co-clustering experiments.

claim: Tumors in NSG mice that received empty vector-transduced T cells grew to ethical endpoint (1000 mm3) within 14 days.
source: Tumors in mice that received empty vector-transduced T cells grew to ethical endpoint (1000 mm3) within 14 days, while mice that received proCAR-1, -2, and -3T cells slowed tumor growth with potency that increased with oligomeric state (Figure 5b, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5b.

claim: Mice that received proCAR-1, -2, and -3 T cells slowed tumor growth with potency that increased with oligomeric state.
source: Tumors in mice that received empty vector-transduced T cells grew to ethical endpoint (1000 mm3) within 14 days, while mice that received proCAR-1, -2, and -3T cells slowed tumor growth with potency that increased with oligomeric state (Figure 5b, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5b and supplement.

claim: proCAR-3 provided tumor control that most closely resembled the CD28TM reference CAR T cells.
source: proCAR-3 provided control that most closely resembled the CD28TM reference CAR T cells.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the in vivo data.

claim: The CD28TM mutant CAR tracked with proCAR-2 and proCAR-3 in vivo tumor control.
source: The CD28TM mutant CAR tracked with proCAR-2 and proCAR-3 (Figure 5c, Figure 5—figure supplement 1), confirming that mutation of the YSxxxT association motif recapitulated the general proCAR functional profile in vivo as well as in vitro.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5c.

claim: Mutation of the YSxxxT association motif in CD28 TMD recapitulated the general proCAR functional profile in vivo as well as in vitro.
source: The CD28TM mutant CAR tracked with proCAR-2 and proCAR-3 (Figure 5c, Figure 5—figure supplement 1), confirming that mutation of the YSxxxT association motif recapitulated the general proCAR functional profile in vivo as well as in vitro.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from comparing the mutant to proCARs.

claim: Mean tumor size at day 14 post-tumor inoculation shows a strong inverse correlation with proCAR oligomeric state.
source: Analysis of mean tumor size at day 14 post-tumor inoculation (the last day all mice were alive) shows a strong inverse correlation with proCAR oligomeric state (Figure 5d).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5d.

claim: The potency of antitumor CAR T cell activity scales directly with the oligomeric state of the engineered receptor when all other features are equal.
source: These data show for the first time that, all other features being equal, the potency of antitumor CAR T cell activity scales directly with the oligomeric state of the engineered receptor.
evidence: This is stated as a major conclusion from the in vivo experiments.

claim: proMP C4.1 features extensive alanine-based complementary packing.
source: This striking correlation between receptor oligomeric state and functional potency prompted us to push the limits further by designing a tetrameric proMP (proMP C4.1), which features extensive alanine-based complementary packing (Figure 6a).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6a.

claim: The free proMP C4.1 peptide migrates on SDS-PAGE predominantly as a single species at a position indicative of a tetramer.
source: The free proMP C4.1 peptide migrates on SDS-PAGE predominantly as a single species at a position indicative of a tetramer (Figure 6b), consistent with the observation that complementary apolar packing alone can drive stable MP assembly (Mravic et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6b.

claim: Complementary apolar packing alone can drive stable membrane protein assembly.
source: The free proMP C4.1 peptide migrates on SDS-PAGE predominantly as a single species at a position indicative of a tetramer (Figure 6b), consistent with the observation that complementary apolar packing alone can drive stable MP assembly (Mravic et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: HER2 proCAR-4 containing the tetrameric proMP C4.1 TMD sequence was well expressed at the surface of freshly isolated mouse CD8+ T cells.
source: HER2 proCAR-4 containing the tetrameric proMP C4.1 TMD sequence was well expressed at the surface of freshly isolated mouse CD8+ T cells (Figure 6c, Figure 6—figure supplement 1) and supported strong tumor cell killing in vitro (Figure 6d).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6c and supplement.

claim: proCAR-4 supported strong tumor cell killing in vitro.
source: HER2 proCAR-4 containing the tetrameric proMP C4.1 TMD sequence was well expressed at the surface of freshly isolated mouse CD8+ T cells (Figure 6c, Figure 6—figure supplement 1) and supported strong tumor cell killing in vitro (Figure 6d).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6d.

claim: The monomeric proCAR-1 T cells clearly segregated with weaker killing in the live-cell imaging assay at low effector:target ratio.
source: This live-cell imaging assay at low effector:target ratio confirmed that oligomeric proCAR T cells and the T cells expressing the reference CD28TM CAR were all potent killers in vitro, but the monomeric proCAR-1 T cells clearly segregated with weaker killing.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the killing assay.

claim: The scaled killing observed in vivo was not evident in the in vitro killing assay, consistent with observations that in vitro killing is easily saturated.
source: Interestingly, the scaled killing we observed in vivo was not evident here, consistent with observations by others that in vitro killing is easily saturated and some differences in CAR activity are only observed at very low target antigen density (Majzner et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as an observation with a supporting citation.

claim: In vivo, proCAR-4 T cells displayed a level of MC38-HER2 tumor control that was indistinguishable from the CD28TM reference CAR-T cells.
source: In vivo, proCAR-4 T cells displayed a level of MC38-HER2 tumor control that was indistinguishable from the CD28TM reference CAR-T cells (Figure 6e, Figure 6—figure supplement 2), thereby closing the functional gap that was apparent between proCAR-3 and the CD28TM CAR in the previous experiment.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6e and supplement.

claim: proCAR-4 closed the functional gap that was apparent between proCAR-3 and the CD28TM CAR in tumor control.
source: In vivo, proCAR-4 T cells displayed a level of MC38-HER2 tumor control that was indistinguishable from the CD28TM reference CAR-T cells (Figure 6e, Figure 6—figure supplement 2), thereby closing the functional gap that was apparent between proCAR-3 and the CD28TM CAR in the previous experiment.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the in vivo data.

claim: proCAR-4 T cells released significantly lower levels of cytokines than the CD28TM reference CAR T cells in vitro despite functional equivalence in vivo.
source: Despite this functional equivalence in vivo, proCAR-4 T cells still released significantly lower levels of cytokines than the CD28TM reference CAR T cells in vitro (Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: The tetrameric proCAR-4 design trended towards higher levels of all cytokines than the other proCARs.
source: However, the tetrameric design trended towards higher levels of all cytokines than the other proCARs.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the cytokine data.

claim: When cytokine release was normalized to the CD28TM reference across all experiments for all proCAR T cells, the combined data revealed strong linear correlations with receptor oligomeric state for all cytokines tested.
source: When we normalized cytokine release to the CD28TM reference across all experiments for all proCAR T cells, the combined data revealed strong linear correlations with receptor oligomeric state for all cytokines tested (Figure 6f), reflecting a similar relationship to that identified in the in vivo tumor control data.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6f.

claim: The high cytokine release stimulated by the CD28TM CAR is largely determined by recruiting native CD28 through the TMD.
source: Taken together, our results reveal that the high cytokine release stimulated by the CD28TM CAR is largely determined by recruiting native CD28 through the TMD.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the combined experiments.

claim: Amongst the proCAR designs that eliminate interaction with endogenous CD28, the relative cytokine levels scale directly with the receptors' oligomeric state.
source: Yet, amongst the proCAR designs that all eliminate this unintended interaction and thereby reduce cytokine release, the relative cytokine levels scale directly with the receptors' oligomeric state.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the proCAR data.

claim: The scaling of cytokine levels with oligomeric state is consistent with a sensitivity to the number of CAR-encoded CD28 and CD3 tail sequences that can be engaged by a single antigen-binding event.
source: This is consistent with a sensitivity to the number of CAR-encoded CD28 and CD3 tail sequences that can be engaged by a single antigen-binding event.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the mechanism.

claim: Cytokine production in response to HER2-negative tumor cells was very low in all constructs.
source: As expected, cytokine production in response to HER2-negative tumor cells was very low in all constructs (Figure 6g), showing that pre-assembled higher-order oligomers did not cause spontaneous antigen-independent activation of cytokine production and still required stimulation.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6g.

claim: Pre-assembled higher-order oligomers did not cause spontaneous antigen-independent activation of cytokine production and still required stimulation.
source: As expected, cytokine production in response to HER2-negative tumor cells was very low in all constructs (Figure 6g), showing that pre-assembled higher-order oligomers did not cause spontaneous antigen-independent activation of cytokine production and still required stimulation.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the antigen-negative control data.

claim: There is a robust linear correlation between CAR oligomeric state and CAR T cell functional output, both in vivo and in vitro, that extends at least to the tetrameric state.
source: These data confirm a robust linear correlation between CAR oligomeric state and CAR T cell functional output, both in vivo and in vitro, that extends at least to the tetrameric state.
evidence: This is stated as a major conclusion from all the functional data.

claim: The lowest-energy-designed structures systematically exhibited features related to protein misfolding, such as self-assembly through multiple alternative interfaces.
source: Starting from a general methodology for the de novo design of membrane-spanning homodimers, we learned that the lowest-energy-designed structures systematically exhibited features that are related to protein misfolding, such as self-assembly through multiple alternative interfaces.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the design work.

claim: Biochemical and structural analysis noted a surprising tendency of the designs to self-assemble into higher-order oligomers.
source: Furthermore, biochemical and structural analysis noted a surprising tendency of the designs to self-assemble into higher-order oligomers.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from experimental characterization.

claim: A new strategy that incorporated negative design principles into an automated design workflow generated highly expressed and atomically accurate single-span oligomers of defined order.
source: To counter these unexpected problems, we developed a new strategy that incorporated negative design principles into an automated design workflow and generated highly expressed and atomically accurate single-span oligomers of defined order.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the methodological development.

claim: The formation of SDS-resistant peptide complexes consistent with the target oligomeric state is indicative of high stability.
source: Their formation of SDS-resistant peptide complexes consistent with the target oligomeric state is indicative of high stability.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the SDS-PAGE data.

claim: The excellent agreement of SDS-PAGE analysis with design models and experimentally determined structures indicates that the designed interfaces dominate.
source: While this analysis does not rule out unintended weak interactions that are disrupted by denaturants, its excellent agreement with design models and experimentally determined structures indicates that the designed interfaces dominate.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the combined data.

claim: Using natural TMDs can confound predictability and control by encoding unexpected functions.
source: The outcomes of the proCAR design experiments revealed two specific mechanistic insights into engineered immune receptor function. First, our results highlight how using natural TMDs can confound predictability and control by encoding unexpected functions.
evidence: This is stated as a major insight from the work.

claim: In the HER2 CAR, CD28 costimulation is explicitly encoded through the CD28 signaling tail and also amplified through a specific sequence signature in the CD28 TMD that recruits endogenous CD28.
source: In the HER2 CAR used here, CD28 costimulation is explicitly encoded through the CD28 signaling tail incorporated into the CAR protein but is also amplified through a specific sequence signature in the CD28 TMD that recruits endogenous CD28 into activated CAR complexes.
evidence: This is stated as a mechanistic finding from the study.

claim: A dimeric CAR incorporating the CD28 TMD has the potential to recruit two dimers of endogenous CD28, contributing as many as four additional costimulatory sequences.
source: A dimeric CAR incorporating the CD28 TMD thus has the potential to recruit two dimers of endogenous CD28, contributing as many as four additional costimulatory sequences to a receptor that carries only two within the CAR sequence itself.
evidence: This is stated as an inference about the stoichiometry of the interaction.

claim: Additional costimulatory signaling from recruited endogenous CD28 likely explains a large portion of the enhanced potency and higher toxicity of CD28 TMD-containing CARs.
source: This additional costimulatory signaling, which supports both cell division and cytokine production, likely explains a large portion of the enhanced potency and higher toxicity of CD28 TMD-containing CARs compared to those that use TMDs from CD8 or other proteins (Majzner et al., 2020; Fujiwara et al., 2020; Brudno et al., 2020; Cappell and Kochenderfer, 2021; Davey et al., 2020) and underscores the importance of fully understanding the structure–function relationships in natural TMDs when repurposing them for receptor engineering.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation with supporting citations.

claim: Systematic and robust interrogation of the relationship between oligomeric state and CAR function has never before been possible.
source: The second major mechanistic insight from this study is that CAR T cell functional potency scales directly with the immune receptor's oligomeric state when all other features are equal. Systematic and robust interrogation of this relationship has never before been possible because type I single-spanning TMDs with well-characterized oligomeric structures are limited (Trenker et al., 2016) and functional outcomes that depend strictly on oligomeric state are not easily separated from other features and functions of TMDs (Bridgeman et al., 2010; Bridgeman et al., 2014; Wan et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations explaining the limitations of prior work.

claim: De novo-designed proMPs provided a panel of well-characterized, orthogonal TMDs that enabled the finding that CAR potency scales with oligomeric state.
source: Our de novo-designed proMPs provided a panel of well-characterized, orthogonal TMDs that enabled this finding.
evidence: This is stated as the key contribution of the proMP technology.

claim: Other structural aspects of receptor complexes, such as TMD geometry or conformational changes, could in principle have roles in receptor activity levels.
source: Other structural aspects of the receptor complexes, such as the TMD geometry or conformational changes transmitted from the extracellular ligand-binding domains to the intracellular signaling domains, could in principle have roles in receptor activity levels; however, the observed linear relation between oligomeric state and activation suggests that these other aspects play minor roles, if any.
evidence: This is stated as a consideration and interpretation of the results.

claim: The observed linear relation between oligomeric state and activation suggests that other structural aspects play minor roles, if any.
source: Other structural aspects of the receptor complexes, such as the TMD geometry or conformational changes transmitted from the extracellular ligand-binding domains to the intracellular signaling domains, could in principle have roles in receptor activity levels; however, the observed linear relation between oligomeric state and activation suggests that these other aspects play minor roles, if any.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the linear correlation observed.

claim: The proMP design workflow can provide tools to directly test the role of TMD geometry in CAR signaling by generating different structures of the same oligomeric state.
source: Notably, our proMP design workflow can now provide the tools to directly test the role of TMD geometry in CAR signaling by generating different structures of the same oligomeric state for systematic comparisons in future studies.
evidence: This is stated as a future application of the technology.

claim: The ability to broadly attenuate CAR T cell cytokine release while providing a predictable range of functional potencies may have important implications for developing future cellular immunotherapies.
source: The ability to broadly attenuate CAR T cell cytokine release while providing a predictable range of functional potencies may have important implications for the development of future cellular immunotherapies.
evidence: This is stated as a potential implication of the work.

claim: The most effective CAR T cell therapies are accompanied by dangerously high levels of inflammatory cytokine production that cause cytokine release syndrome (CRS).
source: The most effective CAR T cell therapies are accompanied by dangerously high levels of inflammatory cytokine production that cause CRS, which is characterized by fever, hypotension, respiratory distress, and multiorgan failure that can be fatal if not carefully managed (Morgan et al., 2010; Gutierrez et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: Current clinical practice is to manage CRS symptoms with cytokine-blocking antibodies and corticosteroids.
source: The current clinical practice is to manage CRS symptoms with cytokine-blocking antibodies and corticosteroids (Maus et al., 2020; Morris et al., 2022), but approaches to prevent CRS altogether using cytokine gene disruption or modified CAR constructs are areas of active research (Brudno et al., 2020; Ying et al., 2019; Sterner et al., 2019; Sachdeva et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: Approaches to prevent CRS altogether using cytokine gene disruption or modified CAR constructs are areas of active research.
source: The current clinical practice is to manage CRS symptoms with cytokine-blocking antibodies and corticosteroids (Maus et al., 2020; Morris et al., 2022), but approaches to prevent CRS altogether using cytokine gene disruption or modified CAR constructs are areas of active research (Brudno et al., 2020; Ying et al., 2019; Sterner et al., 2019; Sachdeva et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claim: A tetrameric proCAR has in vivo antitumor activity that precisely matched the potent CD28TM design while providing a 40–60% reduction in inflammatory cytokine release.
source: The lessons we learned from analysis of monomeric, dimeric, and trimeric proCAR designs led to the generation of a tetrameric proCAR with in vivo antitumor activity that precisely matched the potent CD28TM design while still providing a 40–60% reduction in inflammatory cytokine release.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the proCAR-4 results.

claim: Other proCAR designs offer greater reductions in cytokine release but also exhibit concomitant loss of antitumor activity in vivo.
source: Other proCAR designs offer greater reductions in cytokine release but also exhibit concomitant loss of antitumor activity in vivo.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the trade-offs observed.

claim: The complete proCAR panel provides an opportunity to better balance safety and efficacy in CAR T cell therapies by selecting from a spectrum of designs with defined structure–function relationships.
source: The complete proCAR panel thus provides an opportunity to better balance safety and efficacy in CAR T cell therapies by selecting from a spectrum of designs with defined structure–function relationships.
evidence: This is stated as a potential application of the work.

claim: Fully assessing the clinical potential of proCARs will require further testing in mouse models that more closely approximate treatment of established disease in patients.
source: Fully assessing their clinical potential will require further testing in mouse models that more closely approximate treatment of established disease in patients, support longer-term persistence studies, and allow direct measurement of cytokine toxicity in vivo.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation and future direction.

claim: TMD modifications do not directly impact either the antigen-binding or signaling domains.
source: Importantly, TMD modifications do not directly impact either the antigen-binding or signaling domains.
evidence: This is stated as an advantage of the modular design approach.

claim: The modularity of TMDs means that proMP TMDs may be easily implemented on the background of any existing single-chain receptor design.
source: This modularity means that proMP TMDs may be easily implemented on the background of any existing single-chain receptor design and can be combined with other modifications in extracellular or intracellular sequences to expand the combinatorial space available for fine-tuning signaling outputs.
evidence: This is stated as a potential application of the technology.

claim: The flexibility of proMP TMDs should facilitate screening for an optimal design for each tumor type and target antigen.
source: This flexibility should facilitate screening for an optimal design for each tumor type and target antigen.
evidence: This is stated as a potential benefit of the approach.

claim: The proMP design methods and sequences will find additional applications for controlling intermolecular cell-surface protein interactions in a variety of synthetic and biological systems.
source: We anticipate that the proMP design methods and sequences will find additional applications for controlling intermolecular cell-surface protein interactions in a variety of synthetic and biological systems.
evidence: This is stated as an anticipated future application.
